points.en: The ground of ethics is God's holiness, the very purity of who He is, not a rule He keeps.
The reason for the standard is God's own nature ("be holy, for I am holy"), not usefulness or community needs.
His commands are the overflow of His perfect character, so ethics must begin with who God is.
Error one: things are good merely because God arbitrarily commands them, making God a tyrant and goodness a coin-flip.
Error two: things are good by a standard above God that even He must obey, making God a servant of a higher law.
Biblical answer: a thing is good because it reflects God's unchanging character; goodness is neither arbitrary nor above Him.
Every human being is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27).
Therefore each person has a worth that cannot be earned, diminished or revoked, because it is grounded in God and not in the person.
Worth does not rise or fall with usefulness, health, morality or agreement; it governs sanctity of life, the poor and church discipline.
Ceremonial law governed sacrifice and temple and pointed to Christ, so it is fulfilled in Him.
Civil law ordered the nation of Israel and was given to a particular nation and time.
Moral law expresses God's unchanging will and abides, because it is rooted in God's own nature.
This is why the church teaches the Ten Commandments but no longer offers lambs.
Christ came not to destroy or soften the Law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17).
He drives the law inward from outward behavior to the heart, thoughts and intents, such as anger behind murder and lust behind adultery.
This is progressive revelation at its summit: the full unveiling of what the law always meant, not a contradictory standard.
No one can keep the law by himself, because there is none righteous (Romans 3:10).
The law is not a ladder to reach God but a mirror that shows our sin and drives us in despair to the cross.
The law diagnoses but cannot cure; the cure is the gospel, where Christ satisfies its demand and pays its penalty.
Holiness is the fruit of the Spirit, produced by the Spirit's work, not the achievement of human effort (Galatians 5:22-23).
Fruit grows as the vine's life flows through the branch, so character is grown in a soul united to Christ and not forced by willpower.
Grace comes before obedience: we obey because we are already accepted, not in order to be accepted, and the power to obey is itself a gift.
Reversing the order produces either a Pharisee or a wreck.
Kept straight, obedience is the glad response of a son to a Father who has already embraced him.
The method asks what the human author, led by the Spirit, meant to his original readers by his words in their setting, and only then applies the truth to us.
A wax nose is a text bent to fit one's preferences or prior plans, which uses the Word instead of honoring it.
Read the verse in its paragraph, the paragraph in its book, and the book in the whole counsel of God.
The three families locate the good in character (virtue), duty and rule (deontology), and consequences (utilitarianism).
Each grasps something real because each borrows from God's moral order; Scripture cares about character, duty and consequences.
Each fails by tearing its fragment loose from God to carry all of morality; the Christian gathers the truth in each and orders it under God's revelation.
